hook: The Indian astronomer who said the Earth spins, and helped give the world its numbers.

pages.x: Aryabhata was born in 476, and wrote that he finished his great book at the age of 23, in 499. He worked at Kusumapura, near Pataliputra, then a centre of learning of the Gupta Empire, the golden age of classical India.

His book, the Aryabhatiya, packs mathematics and astronomy into 121 short verses, easy to learn by heart. It covers arithmetic, algebra and trigonometry, and how to work out the movements of the Sun, Moon and planets.
He gave pi as 62,832 divided by 20,000, which is 3.1416, and said it was only close. He wrote numbers in a place-value system, where a digit's position gives its worth.
pages.fx: Indian place-value numbers with zero, carried west by Arab scholars, became the digits the whole world uses today.

pages.x: He said the Earth turns on its axis every day, and the stars only seem to move, as the shore seems to move to a man in a boat. He explained eclipses as shadows.
pages.fx: Most astronomers rejected the spinning Earth for 1,000 years, but his tables for predicting eclipses and planets were used across India and the Islamic world.

pages.x: In 1975 India launched its first satellite and named it Aryabhata. A picture of it was printed on India's two-rupee note.

Aryabhata was the first of the great mathematician astronomers of classical India. His work on numbers, pi, sines and the turning Earth was translated into Arabic and shaped the mathematics of the Islamic world and Europe.
pts: Said the Earth spins on its axis
